title: What do multiple arrests in Indonesia mean for Europe's biofuels policy?
description:
An unheard of industry by-product had become a key ingredient of Europe’s transport energy transition almost overnight.
If crude palm oil was indeed being exported as POME, the implications go far beyond tax evasion in Indonesia.
In other words, Europe’s energy transition increasingly depends on supply chains it cannot directly police.
A moment of truth for EU biofuels policy The Indonesian arrests should mark a turning point.
For years, Europe’s renewable transport strategy has leaned heavily on the idea that waste-based biofuels can scale quickly without environmental downsides.
text:
Handcuffed, masked and clad in a pink vest, Fadjar Donny Tjahjadi, the Indonesian Technical Director of Customs, is led towards a prison vehicle. Alongside ten other suspects, including two civil servants and eight private industry players, he stands accused of facilitating the export of hundreds of millions of euros worth of crude palm oil, illegally mislabelled as Palm Oil Mill Effluent (POME).

Still in custody, the suspects face charges of tax evasion that could carry sentences of up to life in prison.

As reported today by investigative journalists, Source Material, those arrested have been supplying POME to the EU’s top biofuel producers, including Eni, Repsol and Neste.

For European policymakers, the images should be striking. Waste biofuels have been a big part of Europe's green energy transition. Most recently, they have been utilised in the push back against the CO2 regulation as an offset option for car manufacturers to continue selling internal combustion engines after 2035.

But for years, NGOs, industry insiders and several EU governments have warned that something was wrong with the bloc’s rapidly growing consumption of imported waste-based biofuels.

Now, those concerns have come to a head.

Europe’s favourite biofuel feedstock

Over the past five years, the EU’s biofuels market has undergone a profound transformation.

In 2019, the EU decided to phase out the use of palm oil in biofuels due to its links with deforestation and land-use change. Attention immediately turned to biofuels made from “waste” materials, such as POME and Used Cooking Oil (UCO), which, in theory, should not drive additional land demand.

However, the sudden surge in demand raised an obvious question: how much of this stuff actually exists?

Between 2022 and 2025, Europe’s consumption of biofuels made from imported POME skyrocketed, rapidly turning the obscure residue into the one of the largest feedstocks for green fuels like Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO) and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

An unheard of industry by-product had become a key ingredient of Europe’s transport energy transition almost overnight.

Growing doubts

Concerns about the integrity of these supply chains did not appear suddenly. They have been building for years. Early warning signs were raised as far back as 2021, when T&E published its first report on UCO, labelling the reliance on the feedstock as “dubious”. This was then followed in 2023, when T&E highlighted how Europe’s rapidly growing reliance on imported waste was creating strong incentives for fraud and mislabelling.

The following year, two deep dives on UCO imports further raised concerns about both the available supply of UCO and of the certification system responsible for verifying the feedstock.

The issue was raised politically within the EU, with both Belgium and Ireland raising the question of fraud at the EU Council, warning that both UCO and POME supply chains are vulnerable to manipulation.

All of these events led to T&E’s most significant publication on the matter. In 2025, T&E report, “Palm oil in disguise” showed clearly how Europe’s consumption of waste-based biofuels appears to exceed plausible global supply, arguing that palm oil may well be entering the EU market disguised as waste feedstocks.

The Indonesian arrests arrive shortly afterwards.

Why the arrests matter for Europe

The investigation in Indonesia suggests that these warnings were justified.

If crude palm oil was indeed being exported as POME, the implications go far beyond tax evasion in Indonesia. It would mean that fuels counted as “advanced” or “waste-based” in Europe may in reality have been produced from the very crop the EU sought to phase out.

That matters because EU biofuel policy is built on a strict hierarchy of feedstocks. Crop-based fuels face caps and restrictions. Waste-based fuels, by contrast, receive generous incentives and can count multiple times their value towards renewable energy targets.

The system assumes that regulators can reliably distinguish between the two. This assumption has finally been officially upended.

A structural problem

The problem is not necessarily limited to one country or one investigation. The structure of the market itself creates powerful incentives for mislabelling.

Waste-based biofuels command a premium because they count more towards climate targets. Meanwhile, verifying the origin of residues thousands of kilometres away is notoriously difficult, if not impossible.

As former EU Commissioner for Energy, Kadri Simson, admitted in 2024, European authorities lack the legal powers to inspect facilities outside the EU. In other words, Europe’s energy transition increasingly depends on supply chains it cannot directly police.

“As you know, the European Commission doesn’t have a mandate to trace the sources in third countries” - Former EU Energy Commissioner Kadri Simson, speaking to the Council of the EU in 2024.

A moment of truth for EU biofuels policy

The Indonesian arrests should mark a turning point.

For years, Europe’s renewable transport strategy has leaned heavily on the idea that waste-based biofuels can scale quickly without environmental downsides. The explosive growth of waste imports post-2019 confirmed that narrative.

Now the EU must face an uncomfortable reality. The apparent abundance of “sustainable” biofuel feedstocks could be, at least partly, an illusion.

That raises difficult questions for policymakers.

How can Europe tighten verification rules for imported waste feedstocks? Should limits be placed on high-risk materials such as POME and imported UCO?

Or more importantly, how can the bloc accelerate the shift toward electrification and truly low-risk fuels?

From scandal to policy shift?

The images from Jakarta of a senior customs official in handcuffs, accused of facilitating biofuel fraud are not going to fade quickly.

They are a stark reminder that climate policy does not operate in a vacuum. When millions of euros in incentives meet opaque global supply chains, the risk of abuse grows.

For Europe, the question is no longer whether fraud is possible. It is now clear it is happening.

The question should be whether the current biofuels system is robust enough to prevent it or whether the POME arrests are just the first crack in a much larger story.

title: Norwegian starts permanent use of 40% SAF on new Danish domestic route
description:
Norwegian has launched a new Danish domestic daily route between Aalborg and Copenhagen that will be the first in Europe to use sustainable aviation fuel on a permanent basis.
The route has been created through a tender under the Danish government’s ‘Green Aviation’ agreement in which the state is actively supporting the use of more SAF.
Emissions from the route are expected to be reduced by more than 3,000 tonnes of CO2 on a lifecycle basis.
In addition to the airline and St1, the collaboration includes Aalborg Airport, fuel supplier DCC & Shell Aviation Denmark and Norwegian fuel supplier AFSN.

text:
Norwegian has launched a new Danish domestic daily route between Aalborg and Copenhagen that will be the first in Europe to use sustainable aviation fuel on a permanent basis. A 40% blend will be used on all departures in 2026 and 2027, with the SAF consisting of European raw materials and produced by Finnish energy company St1 at its biorefinery in Gothenburg, Sweden. The route has been created through a tender under the Danish government’s ‘Green Aviation’ agreement in which the state is actively supporting the use of more SAF. Emissions from the route are expected to be reduced by more than 3,000 tonnes of CO2 on a lifecycle basis. Meanwhile, Norwegian is fighting through the courts a NOK 400 million ($40m) penalty incurred for non-compliance with the EU Emissions Trading System during Covid-19 and the airline’s reconstruction process.

Norwegian says the purpose of the new route is to speed up production of SAF and make it more accessible through demand and building dedicated supply chains, while strengthening Europe’s security of supply. In addition to the airline and St1, the collaboration includes Aalborg Airport, fuel supplier DCC & Shell Aviation Denmark and Norwegian fuel supplier AFSN. The SAF, certified under ISCC sustainability standards, is sold via DCC & Shell Aviation, with AFSN facilitating the transaction structure.

“This is not just a new route. It is a new model for how we accelerate the restructuring of aviation because it creates demand for SAF. In this way, we get volume, and volume is what drives investments and production,” said Geir Karlsen, CEO of Norwegian.

“The Danish state has chosen to use market forces actively. We are proud to have won the tender with the lowest price per tonne of CO2 saved and have been able to deliver documented evidence.”

St1 is supplying the SAF under a three-year agreement and will be blended and delivered through existing aviation fuel infrastructure.

“This is scheduled commercial traffic operating with a stable SAF supply,” said Henrikki Talvitie, CEO of St1. “For a producer, that makes all the difference. Long-term agreements allow us to plan feedstock sourcing, refining volumes and logistics in a responsible way.”

The company’s biorefinery, a joint venture with SCA, is located next to the St1 refinery and has an annual production capacity of 200,000 tons of biofuels, including SAF, renewable diesel, bio-naphtha and bio-LPG. It is designed to process a variety of raw materials, including used cooking oil, fatty food waste and crude tall oil fractions such as fatty acids.

In another collaboration with SCA, St1 is developing Biorefinery Östrand, a large-scale biorefinery that will utilise by-products from the Nordic forest industry and renewable power, and is expected to have an annual production capacity exceeding 200,000 tons of biofuels and e-fuels.

Meanwhile, Norwegian has announced its intention to appeal to Norway’s Supreme Court a decision by the Borgarting Court of Appeal – one of the country’s six intermediate appeals courts – that overturned a previous ruling in Norwegian’s favour from the Oslo District Court. The dispute centres on Norwegian’s EU Emissions Trading System obligations for 2020 at a time when the airline was in a reconstruction process following difficulties encountered during the Covid-19 crisis.

Norwegian maintains that it was legally unable to fulfil the obligations during its court-mandated reconstruction. The airline has already paid the approximate NOK 400 million penalty in 2023 to avoid enforcement but reserved the right to claim a full refund plus interest pending a final legal conclusion.

Accelerating the scale-up of sustainable aviation fuel

Siemens and the ‘cleantech’ company Caphenia have entered a partnership to scale the production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), a synthetic kerosene made from renewable feedstocks that can reduce CO2 emissions by up to 80% compared to ‘fossil kerosene’. Siemens will provide digitalisation and automation solutions for Caphenia’s plasma technology, which ‘converts bio-methane into synthesis gas’. Their aim is a standardised concept that enables the global rollout of commercial production facilities.

Caphenia’s technology uses a plasma process to split bio-methane into synthesis gas at temperatures of around 1,500°C. The company’s Plasma Boudouard Reactor (PBR) is a three-in-one zone reactor that integrates three established chemical reactions in one system. The resulting synthesis gas can then be further processed into SAF, renewable diesel, or chemical products — without by-products and with minimal energy losses.

Christian Gückel, head of ‘Vertical Chemicals’ at Siemens Digital Industries, said: “Decarbonising aviation cannot be achieved without synthetic fuels. Demand for SAF is growing exponentially, yet production capacity urgently needs to be ramped up. This is exactly where Siemens comes in: with our digitalisation and automation solutions, we are making Caphenia’s technology industrially scalable and thus accelerating its global market ramp-up.”

Mark Misselhorn, Caphenia’s founder and CEO, added: “This partnership shows how technology leaders are working together to drive forward the energy transition. Siemens brings the portfolio and expertise to standardise and digitalise our plants. However, the market for SAFs will not grow evenly — it will fragment. Those that scale quickly, are industrial-ready, and have the right partners will lead. Together, we are not only laying the foundation for the international ramp-up of our PBR technology — we want to lead it.”

Under the agreement, Siemens becomes Caphenia’s preferred supplier and technology partner, offering solutions from its Siemens Xcelerator portfolio, including process control systems, drive technology, measurement technology, and process simulation software. Digital twins will make it possible to optimise operating parameters before physical commissioning and to manage processes consistently across different sites.

title: Lufthansa sees 'growing demand' for sustainable fares | Business Travel News Europe
description:
Around seven million Lufthansa Group passengers booked more sustainable travel options in 2025, while nearly 1,700 companies also participated in the airline firm's green initiatives.
This was a significant improvement on 2021 when less than 0.1 per cent of passengers booked a more sustainable ticket.
Lufthansa added in a statement that the volume of SAF (sustainable aviation fuel) sold across its initiatives more than doubled last year compared with 2024.
So far, more than four million passengers have booked a Green Fare, according to Lufthansa.
Dieter Vranckx, chief commercial officer of Lufthansa Group, added: “The growing demand for our more sustainable flying options confirms that we are on the right track.
text:
Around seven million Lufthansa Group passengers booked more sustainable travel options in 2025, while nearly 1,700 companies also participated in the airline firm's green initiatives.

The group, which also includes Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, Eurowings, ITA Airways and Swiss, said that more than 5 per cent of travellers had booked a more sustainable flight option last year, including its "Green Fares". This was a significant improvement on 2021 when less than 0.1 per cent of passengers booked a more sustainable ticket.

Lufthansa added in a statement that the volume of SAF (sustainable aviation fuel) sold across its initiatives more than doubled last year compared with 2024.

Lufthansa’s Green Fares include compensation for carbon emissions within the ticket price through the use of alternative aviation fuels and contributions to climate protection projects. They were first launched as a pilot scheme in 2022, before being made available on European flights the following year and later expanded globally in 2024. So far, more than four million passengers have booked a Green Fare, according to Lufthansa.

Corporates have also been targeted by Lufthansa as part of its sustainability strategy, with companies able to purchase larger quantities of SAF. For example, an investment of €2,000 will allow the corporate to receive a Scope 3 certificate for CO2 emissions savings from flights taken by its travellers.

The airline group said that more than 1,680 companies globally contributed towards alternative aviation fuels during 2025.

Dieter Vranckx, chief commercial officer of Lufthansa Group, added: “The growing demand for our more sustainable flying options confirms that we are on the right track. Every contribution from our passengers increases the use of sustainable aviation fuels in our network and reduces CO2 emissions.”

“We continuously develop our portfolio to make more sustainable flying even easier and more attractive. We are demonstrating that this is not just a vision, but already an established option today.”

Lufthansa said it would continue to add more sustainability options for customers — Green Fares were made available for group bookings of more than nine passengers on long-haul flights in January.

“We continuously develop our portfolio to make more sustainable flying even easier and more attractive,” said Vranckx. “We are demonstrating that this is not just a vision, but already an established option today.”

text:
Oil giant Eni and jet fuel seller Neste among biofuels makers that bought from suppliers targeted by fraud investigation

Indonesian companies targeted in a palm oil fraud probe supplied European firms including Italian energy giant Eni and Finnish sustainable aviation fuel leader Neste, an investigation by SourceMaterial and AFP has found.

Police last month detained 11 people on suspicion of bribing officials to help them disguise palm oil as a less strictly regulated byproduct called palm oil mill effluent, or POME, Indonesia’s attorney general’s office said.

There is no suggestion that Eni, Neste or other companies supplied by the Indonesian businesses implicated in the probe had knowledge of or involvement in any wrongdoing.

Biofuels are a cornerstone of the European Union’s climate strategy that aims to power 29 per cent of cars and planes with ‘green’ energy by 2030. But they can also cause environmental damage and both Eni and Neste have promised to stop importing palm oil because of links to deforestation.

The arrests raise questions about buyers and regulators’ ability to detect fraud and stand by their environmental commitments, said Cian Delaney of Transport & Environment, a campaign group.

“Verification and certification of these imports is clearly failing,” he said. “European Union climate policy that is supposed to promote green fuels is being cheated.”

“EU climate policy that is supposed to promote green fuels is being cheated.”

An Eni spokeswoman said that all of the 21 consignments it received from Green Product International, one of the Indonesian suppliers named by police, contained POME, not palm oil. Eni has “a zero-tolerance policy for regulatory breaches” and immediately suspended all connections with the companies involved, she said.

Neste also removed Green Product International from its supply chain the day after the arrests and “continues to monitor the developments related to the case”, the company said in an emailed statement.

Even before the arrests, the Indonesian government had long suspected fraud in the POME industry. In January 2025 it temporarily suspended approvals for new POME exports after trade statistics appeared to show that the country was exporting 10 times more than it could produce.

Some EU states have already acted to prevent palm oil fraud. Last year Ireland’s government restricted the classification of any palm oil products, including POME, as “renewable fuel” because of verification issues. A similar German moratorium comes into force next year.

Verification has now become so problematic that buyers and regulators should be suspicious of any shipment marked as POME, said James Cogan, head of public policy at ClonBio, an Irish biofuel maker.

“I would challenge any POME or POME-based biofuels processor to publish their volumes, sources and paperwork, to allow public and independent scrutiny,” he said.

POME claims

Indonesian authorities accuse a Green Product International shareholder called Tony (many Indonesians have only one name) of fraudulently mislabelling palm oil as POME.

A person who answered a telephone call to Tanimas Edible Oils, which shares an office with Green Product International and where Tony is also a shareholder, confirmed that he had been arrested and declined to comment further.

Green Product International “sources or stores products” from Tanimas, which has also been removed from Neste’s supply chain, according to Neste’s statement. Neste tested its shipments from Green Product International and found them “consistent with palm-derived waste and residues and not with the typical profile of crude palm oil”, the statement said.

“Neste has taken the risk of fraud very seriously already for years and has developed robust methods to mitigate fraud risk,” the Neste statement said.

Between 2023 and 2025, Green Product International was the leading Indonesian supplier of palm oil products to Eni, with the most recent shipment in October, data shows. In the same period it sent at least 27 cargoes to Neste, the Finnish aircraft fuel supplier, as well as two to Kolmar, a Swiss trader, and one each to Cargill, the US commodities multinational, and Repsol, the Spanish oil major.

There is no suggestion that any of the recipients were involved in or had knowledge of any fraudulent activity.

Eni’s spokeswoman said that all of its POME purchases, including those it made from Green Product International through a third-party contractor, are certified under Italian law and by International Sustainability and Carbon Certification, or ISCC.

ISCC is a major EU-certified verifier of the bloc’s imports of palm oil products for biofuels.

A spokesperson for ISCC said that one of Eni and Cargill’s suppliers targeted by the investigation is “currently excluded from recertification” and another was “previously excluded”.

Green Product International still holds a valid certificate, according to the ISCC’s online registry.

An official at Indonesia’s attorney general’s office confirmed on 4 March that Tony was still in custody along with two other men, Van Ricardo and Erwin, directors of Surya Inti Primakarya and Bumi Mulia Makmur.

Signed customs documents and trade data record Van Ricardo and Erwin’s companies as suppliers of POME to Eni and Cargill in 2023 and 2024.

Neither Surya Inti Primakarya nor Bumi Mulia Makmur responded to calls or messages requesting comment.

Orangutan capital

The northern end of the island of Sumatra, where Green Product International has its headquarters, contains some of the world’s most deforested regions. It is also the only place where Sumatran orangutans, rhinos, Asian elephants and tigers still live together in the wild.

Its Tripa peatland, once known as “the orangutan capital of the world”, has shrunk by 86 per cent since the turn of the millennium as the forest is razed for palm plantations. An orangutan population of 60,000 in the 1980s has dwindled to about 30 today, according to Ian Singleton, conservation manager at Orangutan Haven in North Sumatra.

“It’s devastating,” he said. “Once you chop the forest down, the orangutans have nowhere to live.”

Tony, the arrested shareholder of Green Product International, and a second Green Product International director, are also directors of another company in the region, Inno-Wangsa Oils & Fats.

In November 2022, Inno-Wangsa bought palm oil from two companies that had drained peatlands and cut down rainforest in Tripa, according to documents obtained by Rainforest Action Network, a campaign group.

While much of the felling was legal, both suppliers were fined by the government in 2014 and 2018 for burning forests. That punishment has done little to stem the destruction, said Singleton.

Images collected by Nusantara Atlas show the extent of the deforestation at the SPS II concession

“We were really proud of getting those convictions,” he said. “But on the ground it didn’t really make a lot of difference.”

Satellite images reviewed by SourceMaterial show that deforestation in the site operated by one of the companies from which Inno-Wangsa bought palm oil, SPS II, was amongst the highest in Indonesia in the last year.

Verification challenge

Brussels has set targets requiring airports to make at least 70 per cent of aviation fuel ‘sustainable’ by 2050 and companies like Eni and Neste hope to supply much of that market.

Eni processes around one million tonnes of biofuels feedstock annually and last year signed a five-year deal to supply Ryanair with up to 100,000 tonnes of sustainable aviation fuel.

Neste already supplies jet fuel to some of the world’s biggest airports, including Schiphol in Amsterdam, Los Angeles International and Singapore, and in October extended a multi-year deal with United Airlines.

If deforestation-linked palm oil enters European supply chains, the climate benefits claimed for biofuels may be undermined, said Delaney of Transport & Environment.

“Disguising palm oil as waste products like POME has been far too easy,” he said. “The EU cannot keep relying on the current system.”

title: An Improved Flame Volume Mixing Method for Lean Blowout Prediction of Sustainable Aviation Fuels
authors: Tian Deng, Pengjing Du, Yaobo Li, Xiaojun Yang
description:

There is a mutual coupling relationship between the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio and the dimensionless flame volume in the lean blowout state, and the final LBO limit prediction value needs to be obtained by setting the initial fuel-to-air ratio.
This study does not consider heat transfer between the combustion chamber and the outside environment; therefore, the combustion chamber walls are set as adiabatic, no-slip walls.

Submission received: 3 February 2026 / Revised: 5 March 2026 / Accepted: 7 March 2026 / Published: 16 March 2026

Abstract

This study investigates the fuel discrimination capability of the flame volume mixing method (FV mixing method) in predicting the lean blowout (LBO) limits of different fuels. Conventional FV-based models exhibit limited sensitivity to variations in fuel properties, especially under lean conditions and for sustainable aviation fuels. In this work, an improved FV mixing method is proposed by replacing the classical droplet evaporation treatment with the Abramzon–Sirignano droplet evaporation model, which accounts for fuel-dependent liquid properties, Stefan flow, and coupled convective heat and mass transfer between the gas phase and droplets. As a result, the proposed method shows enhanced sensitivity to fuel variability and improves the prediction accuracy of the LBO limit for the sustainable aviation fuel Cat-C1. The model performance is validated through numerical simulations and compared with experimental data. The results indicate that, compared with the baseline FV mixing method, the proposed approach reduces the LBO prediction error by 5.7%. The improved FV mixing method provides a more robust framework for LBO prediction, with potential applications in fuel characterization and combustion optimization.

1. Introduction

The rapid development of the aviation industry has brought increasingly severe carbon emission challenges. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) can substantially reduce lifecycle emissions compared with conventional jet fuels [1], making it a promising alternative to traditional aviation fuel in the future. However, with the development of aviation engines towards high temperature and lean combustion, the working environment of the combustion chamber gradually approaches the limit of lean blowout (LBO), which may cause problems such as oscillatory combustion and even lean blowout, seriously threatening flight safety [2]. Therefore, it is necessary to accurately grasp the key parameters of the LBO limit to ensure that the combustion state of the engine is always within the safe threshold. The current LBO limit obtained through experimental testing has limitations, such as long testing cycles and high costs. In contrast, the LBO limit prediction method can efficiently obtain the LBO limit of the fuel by knowing the physical properties of the fuel, greatly reducing the experimental measurement steps and research and development costs. Therefore, building LBO rapid prediction models has become a key technological breakthrough in promoting SAF engineering applications and aviation engine safety design.

At present, the mainstream methods for predicting the limit of LBO mainly include semi-empirical models, numerical simulation methods, and hybrid models. Semi-empirical models can be divided into two categories: Perfectly Stirred Reactor (PSR) and Characteristic Time (CT) models. The earliest Perfectly Stirred Reactor model was proposed by Longwell et al. [3], who found that a vortex-driven recirculation zone forms in the bluff-body wake downstream of the stabilizer, which had high mixing intensity and approximately uniform composition. Therefore, it is proposed to consider the recirculation zone behind the blunt body as a homogeneous and temperature gradient-free reactor. On this basis, in 1985, Lefebvre [4] combined fuel vaporization fraction [5] on the basis of homogeneous mixtures to obtain an LBO correlation under heterogeneous conditions. By comparing with the experimental results of multiple combustion chambers, the accuracy of the prediction formula was verified, with an error of ± 30 % . This prediction formula is one of the most widely recognized LBO limit prediction formulas today. The Characteristic Time model is based on the Damkohler (Da) number and was first proposed by Zukoski and Marble [6] in 1955 in their study of semi-empirical models. In the study, the ignition delay time of the fuel/air mixture is considered as the equivalent value of the time required for shear layer mixing, and the critical condition for LBO is the state where the ignition delay time is equal to the residence time of fuel particles. Plee and Mellor [7] found that the concept of shear layer mixing time was superior to the residence time of fuel in the recirculation zone when processing experimental data. They proposed the concept of droplet evaporation time, which was later validated [8,9,10,11]. Xie et al. [12] conducted visual combustion experiments on swirl combustion chambers to explore the LBO mechanism and found that predicting the LBO characteristics of existing engines by studying combustion volume is not accurate. The research focus should shift to the analysis of flame volume [13]. Subsequently, Xie et al. [14] proposed a flame volume (FV) model and an FV Lean Blowout Limit Correlation based on assumptions.

With the improvement in theoretical foundations and computational abilities, the use of numerical simulation to study LBO has received widespread attention. Numerical simulation can effectively study the conditions of reacting and non-reacting flow fields, capturing the dynamic characteristics of flames approaching the LBO limit. Hu Bin et al. [15,16] used the fuel iterative approximation (FIA) method to obtain the relationship between the LBO limit, flame volume V f , and the mass flow rate m r of return air entering the combustible zone. They successfully predicted the LBO limit with an uncertainty range of 17.5. After further combining it with the FV model, a new hybrid model for predicting the LBO limit was proposed, which improved the prediction accuracy. This method can greatly reduce computation time and obtain the LBO limit in a short period of time. In addition, several studies [17,18,19,20] use the characteristic parameter values of a certain section of the combustion chamber to determine the occurrence of LBO and use the fuel steady-state successive approximation method to predict the LBO limit. The prediction process usually requires a large number of iteration steps.

The hybrid model combines semi-empirical models and numerical simulation methods, which have their respective advantages. Sturgess et al. [21,22,23,24] studied a hybrid model that separates the combustion chamber flow field and combustion field for computation. A relatively simple model is used to obtain representative combustor flow fields, and the resulting flow-field data are then processed to construct a Perfectly Stirred Reactor network. The combustion chamber area is divided into multiple sub-zones, and the local LBO limit of each sub-zone is calculated separately. Finally, the global LBO limit is obtained through data processing. Hu Bin et al. [25] combined the relationship between the LBO limit function obtained through numerical simulation using the FIA method with the FV model to propose a new hybrid model for predicting LBO limits. The model further shortened the prediction cycle of LBO and improved the accuracy of the prediction. Compared with experimental data from the combustion chamber, the average uncertainty in the LBO limit obtained by this hybrid model was 16.5%. In addition, Hu Bin and Wang Zhonghao [26,27,28,29,30] proposed using numerical simulation software such as CHEMKIN to obtain the fuel residence time and chemical reaction time of each subregion in the key reaction zone of the combustion chamber and obtain the local Da number of each subregion, thereby deriving the global Da number and using it as a criterion for the occurrence of lean blowout.

Moreover, the complex composition of SAF and its combustion characteristics differ from those of traditional aviation fuel, leading to the challenge of insufficient fuel discrimination ability in existing lean blowout prediction methods. And the applicability verification process of new fuels often requires many tedious steps, known as the time-consuming and costly qualification/certification process [31]. If the LBO limit value can be quickly obtained, the certification process for new sustainable aviation fuels can be greatly reduced. This article uses numerical simulation methods to compare the accuracy of LBO limit prediction using the fuel flow iteration method, characteristic section method, and flame volume mixing method. Using the Abramzon–Sirignano droplet evaporation model instead of the classical droplet evaporation model, considering the effects of droplet property changes, Stefan flow, and gas heat and mass transfer on droplet evaporation, an improved modified Nusselt number flame volume model is obtained to enhance the predictive method’s ability to distinguish sustainable aviation fuels.

2. Research Methods

2.1. Characteristic Cross-Section Method

The characteristic cross-section method analyzes the combustion stability mechanism from the perspective of energy. When the energy released by the combustion of the fuel–air mixture in the recirculation zone is insufficient to ignite the fresh mixture, LBO occurs. In practical combustors, extinction typically initiates in the main reaction zone and then propagates to the recirculation zone. The temperature changes dramatically in the recirculation zone, so specific variables in the recirculation zone can be used as indicators of lean blowout. The characteristic section method selects a characteristic cross-section located near the boundary of the recirculation zone as the research object, monitors the temperature changes on this section, and uses it as the standard to measure the occurrence of LBO. When the temperature changes on the characteristic section meet certain conditions, it is considered as the occurrence of LBO.

Regarding the shape of the recirculation zone in the combustion chamber, this article selected a characteristic cross-section that is tangent to the recirculation zone at x = 57 mm in the combustion chamber, as shown in Figure 1. The rate of change in the temperature-to-fuel–air ratio on the characteristic cross-section Γ was used as a feature parameter to measure the occurrence of LBO. The temperature-to-fuel–air ratio change rate Γ is defined as follows:

Γ = T n − T n − 1 T n − 1 / φ n − φ n − 1 φ n − 1

(1)

In the formula, Γ : change rate of the temperature-to-fuel–air ratio in the characteristic section, T : average temperature in the characteristic section, and φ : the combustion chamber fuel-to-air ratio. Subscript n represents the current iteration step parameter and subscript n − 1 represents the previous iteration step parameter.

We define the rate of change in the temperature-to-fuel–air ratio Γ > 0.45 as the basis for judging the occurrence of LBO, and the specific prediction process is shown in Figure 2.

2.2. Fuel Flow Iteration Method

The fuel flow iteration method assumes that, under fixed inlet, ambient, and fuel conditions, the flame remains stable [32]. At this point, as the fuel mass flow rate gradually decreases, the combustion efficiency and flame temperature of the combustion chamber decrease, and the ignition distance increases; the ignition point will move downstream of the combustion chamber, resulting in a decrease in temperature in the recirculation zone. According to this principle, when the fuel mass flow rate decreases to a certain value, that is, when the fuel-to-air ratio in the combustion chamber decreases to a critical value, the air–fuel mixture in the recirculation zone cannot be ignited, the temperature drops sharply, and LBO occurs. The basis for judging the fuel flow iteration method for lean blowout is the temperature change rate in the recirculation zone, and the characteristic parameter of the average temperature change rate γ in the recirculation zone is defined. When γ > 3 , LBO occurs. The average temperature change rate in the recirculation zone is defined as follows:

γ = T n − T n − 1 T n − 2 − T n − 1 / φ n − φ n − 1 φ n − 2 − φ n − 1

(2)

In the formula, γ : average temperature change rate in the recirculation zone, T : average temperature in the characteristic section, and φ : fuel–air ratio in the combustion chamber. Subscript n represents the current step parameter, subscript n − 1 represents the previous step parameter, and subscript n − 2 represents the first two step parameters.

Based on the definition of the recirculation zone, its corresponding location can be identified. The recirculation zone is approximately spherical in shape in this study, and its volume varies only weakly with changes in the fuel-to-air ratio. Therefore, to facilitate the subsequent evaluation of the mean temperature within the recirculation zone, it is approximated as an equivalent sphere with a radius of 34 mm in this study. In Figure 3, the region where the axial velocity equals zero is displayed; the green region located between the swirler outlet and the primary fuel injection holes corresponds to the combustor recirculation zone under different fuel-to-air ratios. The detailed procedure of the fuel flow iteration method is illustrated in Figure 4.

2.3. Flame Volume Mixing Model

The flame volume mixing method is a hybrid model based on the flame volume (FV) model proposed by Professor Huang Yong’s team at Beihang University [12]. This method assumes that the flame formed by the combustion of the fuel–air mixture in the combustion chamber under lean blowout conditions will fill the entire combustion chamber. Using numerical simulation methods to obtain the combustion chamber head airflow fraction α and dimensionless flame volume β in the prediction formula, the combustion chamber structural parameters, intake air parameters, and fuel property parameters are input into the lean blowout prediction formula, and the final LBO limit prediction value is obtained through iteration. The above method has the advantages of simplicity, speed, and high calculation accuracy compared to the method of simply obtaining the LBO limit through numerical simulation. Based on the above model, Professor Huang Yong’s team further proposed a formula for predicting flame volume, which is expressed as follows:

q L B O = K α β + 1 − α β 2 ( 1 V C ) ( m ˙ a P 3 1.3 exp ( T 3 / 300 ) ) ( D 0 2 λ e f f L H V )

(3)

In the formula: q L B O is the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio, K is the empirical constant of the combustion chamber structure determined through experiments, V C is the volume of the combustion chamber flame tube, m ˙ a is the mass flow rate of the intake air, P 3 is the intake air pressure, T 3 is the intake air temperature, D 0 is the initial droplet diameter, λ e f f is the effective evaporation coefficient of the droplet, and L H V is the low heating value of the fuel.

According to the flame volume prediction Formula (3), it is necessary to first calculate the parameters of the combustion chamber structure, incoming air, and liquid fuel parameters. For combustion chamber structural terms, the combustion chamber structural constant K is usually considered as a constant [33]. Sun Lei et al. [34] believe that the head airflow fraction α can be represented by the swirler airflow fraction, and by monitoring the changes in the air mass flow rate of each intake duct, the flow fraction α = 0.114 for this type of double radial cyclone is obtained. The specific expression formula for dimensionless flame volume is as follows:

β = V f V C

(4)

where β is the dimensionless flame volume, V f is the flame volume size, and V C is the volume size of the main combustion zone of the combustion chamber.

At normal temperature and pressure, the equivalence ratio of the flammability limits of hydrocarbon fuels is 0.5 – 2.0 , which is mainly affected by pressure, temperature, and the combustion environment. The increase in pressure mainly expands the rich combustion boundary. The expansion effect of temperature on the flammable boundary is relatively small. Therefore, this study considers the region within this equivalence ratio range as the flame volume.

For the incoming air term, the combustion chamber structural constants obtained by Lefebvre when proposing the prediction formula were experimentally estimated under specific incoming air pressure and temperature conditions. When the incoming air conditions change, it will have an impact on the results. Huang Xia et al. [33] proposed that the principle of flow similarity can be used to obtain the equivalent air mass flow rate under different operating conditions. This similarity transformation is based on the assumption that in order to ensure that the lean blowout characteristics in the combustion chamber do not change under a specific operating condition, the inlet Mach number before and after the similarity transformation should not change. According to aerodynamic principles such as the ideal gas state equation, the expression for the mass air flow rate at the inlet of the combustion chamber can be obtained:

m ˙ = C P 3 A T 3 q ( λ )

(5)

In the equation, C can be regarded as a constant term when the working fluid remains constant, A is the inlet area of the combustion chamber, which can be regarded as a constant term when the combustion chamber structure remains constant, and q ( λ ) is related to the Mach number. When the inlet Mach number remains constant, it can also be regarded as a constant term. Therefore, an equivalent relationship can be derived that is only related to the inlet air pressure, temperature, and mass flow rate:

m ˙ T 3 P 3 = m ˙ ′ T 3 ′ P 3 ′

(6)

In the formula, m ˙ represents the actual inlet air flow rate, P 3 represents the actual inlet air pressure, T 3 represents the actual inlet air temperature, m ˙ ′ represents the inlet air mass flow rate after similar changes, P 3 ′ represents the Lefebvre experimental inlet air pressure, and T 3 ′ represents the Lefebvre experimental inlet temperature. The incoming air term can be obtained by taking the inlet air pressure of P 3 = 2.3 atm and the inlet air temperature of T 3 = 495 K . To obtain a similar transformed air mass flow rate m ˙ ′ = 1.37 kg / s , the incoming air term can be determined.

For the parameter term of liquid fuel, Ateshkadi et al. [35] believe that a representative Sauter mean diameter (SMD) can be obtained from the correlation of gas swirl atomizers [36], and the SMD value can be used to replace the initial droplet diameter value in the lean blowout prediction formula. This study used numerical simulation to obtain the droplet diameter distribution in the combustion chamber and the SMD value of RP-3 fuel relative to JP-4 fuel. The effective evaporation constant of RP-3 fuel was obtained as 0.47 in the function curve of Lefebvre’s effective evaporation constant at different boiling points through interpolation.

There is a mutual coupling relationship between the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio and the dimensionless flame volume in the lean blowout state, and the final LBO limit prediction value needs to be obtained by setting the initial fuel-to-air ratio. Among them, the judgment basis of this iterative method is the key parameter ε ≤ 0.1 , and its specific expression is as follows:

ε = q L B O , n − q n q n

(7)

In the formula: q n represents the initial fuel-to-air ratio set at step n and q L B O , n represents the predicted value of the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio obtained through numerical simulation calculation at step n . Among them, ε ≥ 0 means that the initial fuel-to-air ratio should be increased for the next round of commuting. When 0, it means that the initial fuel-to-air ratio should be reduced for the next iteration. Figure 5 shows a flowchart for predicting the LBO limit using the flame volume method.

2.4. Revised Nusselt Number Flame Volume Formula

In comparison to numerous methods for predicting LBO limits, the flame volume method is more accurate in predicting the LBO limits of traditional fuels. However, sustainable aviation fuels with complex compositions have significant differences in properties, such as density, viscosity, and surface tension, compared to traditional aviation fuels, resulting in a significant decrease in the prediction accuracy of this method.

To improve this issue, the Abramzon–Sirignano droplet evaporation model [37] was introduced based on the flame volume model, making the model more sensitive to changes in fuel properties. For the flame volume model, the combustion chamber structure term and incoming air term are obviously independent of the physical properties and sensitivity of the liquid fuel. Through the derivation process of the Lefebvre formula, it was found that the liquid fuel parameter term in the prediction formula is actually derived from the fuel droplet evaporation model [38]. Specifically, Lefebvre combined Spalding’s classic droplet evaporation model [39] with Godsave’s D2 law [40] to obtain the average evaporation rate of a single liquid droplet of liquid fuel over its lifecycle. Equations (8) and (9) are the mathematical expressions of the Spalding evaporation model and Godsave’s D2 law, respectively:

m ˙ F = 2 π D k / c p g ln 1 + B

(8)

In the formula: m ˙ F represents the vaporization rate of the liquid droplet, D represents the diameter of the liquid droplet, k represents the thermal conductivity of the fuel liquid droplet, c p represents the heat capacity of the liquid fuel, and B represents the Spalding mass transfer number.

(9)

In the formula: m F represents the instantaneous evaporation rate of fuel droplets, ρ F represents the fuel density, and λ represents the rate of change in the square of the fuel droplet diameter over time.

3. Numerical Simulation

3.1. Geometric Model and Grid Division

This paper simulates the reactive flow field within the combustion chamber. Considering the high computational cost of modeling the entire annular combustion chamber and the periodic symmetry of the annular structure, only 1/18 of the actual combustion chamber is used as the study object for modeling. The model adopts a specific dual-radial swirl combustion chamber, as shown in Figure 6. The computational domain of the combustion chamber starts from the throat of the upstream diffuser and extends to the flame tube outlet. It covers the inner and outer chambers, the annular region between the inner and outer diffusers, the dual swirl inlet device, and the flame tube (including the swirlers, Venturi tube, main fuel holes, mixing holes, and film holes). The cross-sectional area of the computational domain is shown in Figure 7. The combustion chamber uses a dual-radial counter-swirl system, with the first-stage swirler rotating counterclockwise and the blade installation angle set at 64°, and the second-stage swirler rotating clockwise with a blade installation angle of 70°. The fluid computational domain is set with the airflow inlet at the far left. Fresh air enters the combustion chamber through the main fuel holes and mixing holes, participating in fuel mixing and combustion, and is then exhausted through cooling holes downstream of the combustion chamber. The total length of the computational domain is 339 mm, the height is 150 mm, and the width is 120 mm.

The grid division adopts a mixed structured and unstructured grid. The surface of the model is an unstructured polygonal mesh, while the interior is a structured mesh. Polyhedral meshes are generated on the computational domain surface and complex structured surface areas. Local mesh refinement is applied in the swirler and flame tube region to better resolve complex flow structures. The cross-sectional shape of the grid is shown in Figure 8.

The temperature variation along the X-direction and velocity variation along the Y-direction for different grid numbers of 1.09 million, 2.27 million, 3.60 million, and 5.78 million grids are shown in Figure 9 and Figure 10. Due to the frictional force of the combustion chamber wall on the fluid, a velocity gradient and boundary layer are formed. Comparing the grid cases, it can be observed that coarser grids struggle to capture the velocity development near the combustion chamber wall boundary layer. The temperature distribution along the centerline is generally consistent across different grid numbers, with minimal differences in velocity distribution between the 3.6 million and 4.4 million grid cases. To ensure computational accuracy and efficiency, a grid of 3.6 million is chosen for the subsequent numerical simulations.

To verify the correctness of the computational model used in this article, calculations were performed on the steady-state cold flow field and hot temperature field. Figure 11 shows a comparison between the Y-direction axial distribution at x = 50 mm obtained from the steady-state cold flow field calculation of the dual radial swirl combustion chamber model and the literature [41]. The comparison results show that the numerical simulation calculation results are in good agreement with the literature results, and the axial velocity shows a “bimodal” distribution, with the lowest velocity at the y = 0 position. Due to the significant impact of the temperature in the recirculation zone in front of the main combustion hole on the accuracy of the simulation results of the combustion process, a point on the central axis in front of the main combustion hole was taken to compare the simulation temperature results. As shown in Figure 12, the average error of the simulation results is only 3.97%, so the numerical simulation research in this paper is based on this model.

3.3. Boundary Conditions

The models and comparison methods used in this study are implemented through the built-in models of ANSYS Fluent 2024R1. This study simplifies the fuel atomization process and uses the Discrete Phase Model (DPM) to numerically simulate the atomization of liquid fuel. Fuel injectors are set at the centerline x = 12 m m of the combustion chamber to simulate the injection of liquid aviation fuel into the combustion chamber. The particle breakup model used is the KH-RT model. The calculations are performed using an unsteady implicit solver with the SIMPLE algorithm. A pressure-based approach is used for unsteady state solving, with second-order implicit time discretization and a time step of 2 × 10−5 s, lasting approximately 80 ms, with monitored variables converging.

To evaluate the effect of time discretization errors on the results, a time step sensitivity check is performed. With all other numerical settings kept unchanged, a time-step sensitivity study was conducted using three time-step sizes (1 × 10−5 s, 2 × 10−5 s, and 4 × 10−5 s). The results indicate that the variations in the outlet-plane mean temperature and the pressure drop among the three cases are both within 4%, demonstrating that the selected time-step size provides sufficient accuracy for the simulations reported in this study.

This study does not consider heat transfer between the combustion chamber and the outside environment; therefore, the combustion chamber walls are set as adiabatic, no-slip walls. 4. Results and Discussion

This section first discusses three commonly used methods for predicting LBO limits, namely, the characteristic section method, fuel flow iteration method, and FV mixing method, and analyzes and compares their application effects. The air mass flow rate in the combustion chamber remained constant at 0.9 kg/s. Using traditional aviation fuel RP-3 as the research object, Kunda’s [42] 16-component, 23-step C12H23 simplified combustion reaction mechanism was used to simulate the flow and combustion process in the combustion chamber. Subsequently, the FV flame volume method was optimized.

4.1. LBO Prediction Using the Characteristic Cross-Section Method

Using the characteristic cross-section method, the occurrence of LBO was predicted through several iterations (see Table 2). The results indicate that when the fuel–air ratio is 0.0057, the rate of change in temperature with respect to the fuel–air ratio exceeds 0.45. Moreover, among all iterative cases, only this fuel–air ratio yields a change rate greater than 0.45. Accordingly, the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio is 0.0057. In comparison, Huang Xia [33] obtained an LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio of 0.00497 through numerical simulations under the same operating conditions, with a difference of about 14.7%. It is important to note that during the iteration process, the initial fuel-to-air ratio should be set greater than the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio to avoid iteration convergence to an incorrect value. Additionally, the rate of change in the fuel-to-air ratio between each iteration step should remain appropriate to ensure the stability and accuracy of the numerical solution.

4.2. LBO Prediction Using the Fuel Flow Iteration Method

Using the fuel flow iteration method, the LBO limit was predicted through several iterative calculations. It was found that the average temperature change rate exceeds 3 only when the fuel-to-air ratio is 0.0057. Accordingly, the predicted LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio is 0.0057, which differs by about 14.7% compared to the predicted result obtained by Huang Xia [33]. The specific iteration process is detailed in Table 3. After obtaining the predicted value of the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio, three further iterations were carried out. The results showed that the average temperature change rate in the recirculation zone did not meet the conditions γ > 3 when the fuel-to-air ratio was greater than 0.0057 or less than 0.0057, proving the uniqueness of this characteristic parameter and indicating that there is only one predicted value.

4.3. LBO Prediction Using the Flame Volume Mixing Method

Using the flame volume method, the LBO limit was predicted through four iterations (Table 4). It was found that, at the fourth iteration, the absolute value of the relative error was below 0.1, corresponding to a fuel-to-air ratio of 0.00459. Therefore, the predicted LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio under this operating condition is 0.00459. This value differs from the prediction reported by Huang Xia [33] (0.00497) by approximately 7.6%. Compared with the characteristic cross-section method and the fuel flow iteration method, both of which yield a relative error of 14.7%, the flame volume mixing method provides the closest result to the experimental data among the three methods.

4.4. LBO Prediction Using the Modified Nusselt Number Flame Volume Model

Using the new Cat-C1 fuel, a sustainable aviation fuel produced from alcohol by Gevo [43], as the subject, the combustion field in this dual-radial combustion chamber model is calculated using the 42-component, 656-step reaction surrogate model from Wang et al. [44]. The modified Nusselt number prediction model is used to predict the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio for the fuel. Compared to RP-3, Cat-C1 contains almost no aromatic hydrocarbons, with a composition primarily of isomerized alkanes, a higher H/C ratio, and a significantly lower DCN, reflecting its weaker auto-ignition reactivity. These differences affect spray evaporation and local mixing stratification, as well as the robustness of flame anchoring in the recirculation zone, leading to changes in the LBO limit. Such fuel property-driven differences in LBO behavior have also been discussed in existing studies on gas turbine combustion stability [45].

Figure 13 shows the predicted LBO limits at different inlet temperatures. This trend is consistent with the conclusions obtained in the study by Luo [46]. As the combustion chamber inlet temperature increases from 340 K to 400 K, the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio decreases significantly. This is mainly because, as the inlet temperature increases, the droplet evaporation rate accelerates, fuel spray evaporation becomes more complete, and the fuel–air mixing quality improves. This results in a more easily formed and stable combustible mixture. At the same time, a higher initial temperature also helps shorten ignition delay, enhance the chemical reaction rate, and improve the stability of the flame under near-LBO conditions, thereby reducing the minimum fuel supply required to maintain combustion, which is reflected as a significant decrease in the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio. After the combustion chamber inlet temperature exceeds 400 K, the change in the LBO limit decreases sharply, and as the temperature increases, it gradually stabilizes. This indicates that the impact of inlet temperature on the LBO boundary is highly sensitive in the early stages, but after the temperature reaches a certain range, the improvement effect of droplet evaporation and mixing processes is essentially exhausted, and the marginal gains from further temperature increases are significantly reduced. At this point, the LBO boundary is more constrained by factors such as the combustion chamber flow organization, the flame stabilization capability of the recirculation zone, and residence time. Therefore, its change becomes gradual and eventually stabilizes. The fitted curve of the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio with inlet temperature variation in this combustion chamber model is obtained as:

q L B O = 67.3 e − T 3 / 30.3 + 0.00464

(38)

As the inlet pressure increases, the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio of the combustion chamber gradually decreases (as shown in Figure 14), meaning that increasing the combustion chamber inlet pressure helps improve the LBO performance of the combustion chamber. This conclusion is consistent with that of Suo [47]. The main reason is that when the inlet pressure increases, the gas density in the combustion chamber increases, enhancing the heat and mass transfer processes between the fuel droplets and the surrounding gas, which leads to more complete droplet evaporation and facilitates the formation of a more uniform and stable combustible mixture. At the same time, higher pressure typically increases the chemical reaction rate and enhances the heat release intensity of the flame, thereby improving the stability of the flame under near-LBO conditions and allowing combustion to be maintained even at lower fuel-to-air ratios. However, this change is not linear. As the inlet pressure continues to increase, the decrease in the LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio becomes less pronounced, indicating that the improvement effect of inlet pressure on LBO performance exhibits a clear diminishing marginal effect. This is because, in lower pressure ranges, increasing pressure has a more significant promoting effect on evaporation, mixing, and reaction processes. Once the pressure reaches a certain level, these processes have already been sufficiently improved, and further pressure increases result in limited gains. At this point, the LBO limit is more constrained by factors such as the combustion chamber flow organization, the flame stabilization capability of the recirculation zone, local mixing uniformity, and residence time. Therefore, the effect of increasing inlet pressure on LBO performance gradually saturates. The following fitted curve is obtained:

q L B O = 0.00416 e − P 3 / 1.1 + 0.00424

(39)

To investigate the reason for the nonlinear variation of the LBO limit fuel–air ratio with the inlet pressure shown in Figure 14, the temperature distributions on the central axial plane of the combustor at different inlet pressures with a fuel–air ratio of 0.0050 are presented in Figure 15. Although slight differences in the temperature fields can be observed under different inlet pressures, the overall distributions remain essentially similar. Therefore, the increase in inlet pressure does not significantly enhance the fuel–air mixing and combustion efficiency in the combustor to release more heat. As a result, the lean blowout performance of the combustor is not improved, and the LBO limit fuel–air ratio does not decrease.

In Figure 16, as the inlet pressure increases, the contour of the combustion chamber recirculation zone gradually becomes fuller from the “M” shape, that is, the recirculation zone gradually increases. From a timescale perspective, when the residence time of liquid fuel in the recirculation zone of the combustion chamber is less than the chemical timescale, LBO occurs. An increase in the recirculation zone means that the residence time of liquid fuel particles in the recirculation zone increases, so even without providing additional energy to the combustion chamber, its lean blowout characteristics can be improved.

As the inlet mass flow rate increases, the lean blowout (LBO) limit fuel–air ratio of the combustor gradually increases (Figure 17), indicating that an increase in combustor inlet mass flow rate deteriorates the lean blowout performance. This trend is consistent with that reported by Liu Wei et al. [48]. This is because after the inlet mass flow rate increases, the average flow velocity in the combustor rises, and the fluid residence time in the combustion zone is shortened, thereby reducing the time available for fuel evaporation, fuel–air mixing, and chemical reactions. As a result, under near-LBO conditions, the flame becomes more difficult to sustain stably. Meanwhile, the higher flow velocity enhances flame stretch and flow-induced disturbances, increasing the risks of flame destabilization and blowout. Therefore, a higher fuel supply rate (i.e., a higher fuel–air ratio) is required to maintain combustion stability. The fitted curve obtained is as follows:

q L B O = 0.00211 m ˙ a + 0.00304

(40)

To investigate the reason for the linear variation in Figure 17, we provide Figure 18. It was found that as the inlet mass flow rate of the combustion chamber increases, the overall temperature change on the axial surface of the combustion chamber shows a downward trend. The reasons for the above results can be divided into two aspects. Firstly, as the inlet mass flow rate increases, more cooler air enters the combustion chamber, directly causing the overall temperature field to decrease. A larger gas mixture will carry more energy and be discharged from the combustion chamber outlet, further reducing the combustion chamber temperature and decreasing the lean blowout performance of the combustion chamber. Secondly, a larger mass flow rate means an increase in air velocity, which shortens the residence time of the gas mixture in the combustion chamber. This means that the fuel chemical reaction time remains unchanged, and the residence time of the fuel is shortened, thereby reducing the lean blowout performance of the combustion chamber. Under the combined effect of the above two aspects, the lean blowout performance of the combustion chamber decreases, and the LBO limit air–fuel ratio increases.

According to the modified Nusselt number flame volume model, the global modified Nusselt number Nu Cat − C 1 ∗ = 2.26 for Cat-C1 fuel under this operating condition is obtained, and the predicted results are compared with the original model results. The predicted iteration processes are shown in Table 5 and Table 6.

The results indicate that there is a discrepancy between the Cat-C1 fuel LBO limit fuel-to-air ratios obtained by iterative calculations using the improved prediction model and the original model. Under the same operating conditions, the improved model predicts an LBO limit fuel-to-air ratio of 0.00514, which differs from the experimental value of 0.00548 reported by Esclapez [45] under identical conditions by approximately 6.2%. Compared with the prediction of 0.00483 obtained from the original model, the prediction accuracy is improved by 5.7%.

5. Conclusions

This study compares the accuracy of three lean blowout (LBO) prediction methods using numerical simulations. In response to the bias in LBO prediction caused by the complex physical properties of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), an improved flame volume model based on the Abramzon–Sirignano droplet evaporation model is proposed. The main conclusions are as follows:

Among the three prediction methods, the flame volume mixing method has the highest accuracy in predicting the LBO limit of traditional aviation fuel RP-3, with a deviation of 7.6% from experimental values, significantly better than the characteristic section method and fuel flow iteration method (both with a deviation of 14.7%). Its prediction process is simpler, and its description of the physical mechanism of the combustion process is more realistic.

The existing flame volume models have insufficient resolution ability for SAF, mainly because the classical droplet evaporation model does not fully consider the special properties of SAF in density, viscosity, surface tension, and other physical properties. The modified Nusselt number flame volume model constructed by introducing the Abramzon–Sirignano droplet evaporation model and incorporating the effects of droplet property changes, Stefan flow, and gas–liquid heat and mass transfer significantly improved the prediction accuracy of SAF. Among them, the prediction error of Cat-C1 fuel was reduced by 5.7% compared to the original model, which verified the sensitivity of the improved model to changes in fuel properties.

Improving the model can effectively capture the LBO characteristics of SAF under different operating conditions. As the inlet temperature of the combustion chamber increases, the limit fuel-to-air ratio of LBO first significantly decreases and then tends to stabilize. Increasing the inlet pressure can narrow the LBO limit and improve the lean blowout performance, but the effect gradually saturates with increasing pressure. An increase in the inlet air mass flow rate will expand the LBO limit and reduce lean blowout performance, mainly related to a shortened combustion residence time.

Although the proposed method achieves some improvement in predicting the lean blowout (LBO) limits of sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs), several limitations remain. First, the current reduction in prediction error relative to the baseline FV model is still limited, and broader datasets as well as further model refinement are still needed to improve the method’s performance. Second, only one SAF surrogate fuel (Cat-C1) was validated in this study, and the robustness and generalization capability of the proposed method still need to be further assessed using more SAF types and a wider range of operating-condition datasets. In addition, the combustor walls were treated as adiabatic in the current CFD framework, and wall thermal effects and wall heat loss on LBO behavior were not considered; these effects will be included in future three-cup combustor studies to improve the physical completeness of the analysis. Finally, the model was mainly developed and validated for a specific combustor configuration, and its applicability to other geometries has not yet been sufficiently demonstrated, which requires further validation under different combustor configurations and operating conditions.
